title: Choosing a Dissertation Topic
context: A supervisor meets two postgraduate students to discuss and narrow down their dissertation research topics.

script.speaker: Dr Fenwick
script.text: Thanks for coming in together. Since you're both looking at consumer behaviour this year, I thought it made sense to talk topics at the same time. Ruth, do you want to go first?

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Happy to go first if it helps, but Ruth's probably got more to say at this stage than I have.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Only because I've rewritten mine more times than I'd like to admit.

script.speaker: Dr Fenwick
script.text: That's either very keen or a bad sign. Let's find out which — go on, Ruth.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Sure. I was originally planning to look at how supermarket loyalty cards affect spending habits generally, but the more reading I do, the more I think that's too broad for a dissertation of this length.

script.speaker: Dr Fenwick
script.text: I'd agree with that instinct. What's a narrower angle you could take?

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: What about just looking at one supermarket chain instead of the whole sector?

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Maybe just focusing on one age group — say, whether loyalty schemes influence spending differently among students compared with older shoppers.

script.speaker: Dr Fenwick
script.text: That's much more manageable. Although, thinking about it, comparing two groups means recruiting two separate samples, which is a lot of extra work for a dissertation on this timeline. What if you focused on just one group in depth instead?

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: That would make sense. I'll focus purely on students, then, and go deeper rather than wider.

script.speaker: Dr Fenwick
script.text: Good, that's settled. So the final topic is loyalty scheme influence on student spending specifically, not a comparison across ages.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Yes, that feels much more realistic now.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: That's a good way to put the problem, actually — I've been trying to compare far too much in mine as well.

script.speaker: Dr Fenwick
script.text: Callum, what have you got?

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: I'm interested in online reviews, and how much people trust them. Originally I wanted to look at reviews across several different product categories — electronics, restaurants, clothing.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Electronics and restaurants and clothing all in one dissertation does sound like rather a lot.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: I know. I think I was just trying to keep my options open for as long as possible.

script.speaker: Dr Fenwick
script.text: Again, that sounds like three studies squeezed into one. Is there a category you find more interesting than the others?

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Restaurants, definitely. I keep coming back to that in my reading anyway.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: That's the one you always bring up in seminars anyway.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Is it that obvious?

script.speaker: Dr Fenwick
script.text: Then let's narrow it there. Restaurant reviews specifically — that gives you a single, well-defined context.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Okay. Should I look at trust in reviews generally, or something more specific within that?

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: I read reviews before almost anything now, even things I don't really need advice on.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Same. I'm not sure that's healthy, but here we are.

script.speaker: Dr Fenwick
script.text: What's driving your interest — is it the star rating, the written comments, or something else?

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Honestly, it's the written comments. I think people trust a detailed written comment more than a star rating on its own.

script.speaker: Dr Fenwick
script.text: That's actually a nicely testable claim. So your final topic could be how the presence of a detailed written comment affects trust in restaurant reviews, rather than trust in reviews generally.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Yes, I like that, it's specific enough to actually answer.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: That's a relief — at least we've both got something workable now.

script.speaker: Dr Fenwick
script.text: Good. Now, both of you will need to think about method. Ruth, were you planning a survey, or interviews?

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: I was leaning towards interviews, to get richer detail, but given the numbers I'd need for a solid dissertation, I think a survey makes more sense here.

script.speaker: Dr Fenwick
script.text: Agreed, a survey suits a topic like yours much better than interviews would.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Good — interviews would have taken forever to transcribe anyway.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: What about me? I was thinking a survey too, but now that I think about it, maybe a small experiment would work better, showing people the same restaurant with and without a detailed comment.

script.speaker: Dr Fenwick
script.text: That's a strong idea, actually — an experiment would let you isolate the effect much more clearly than a survey could. Let's go with that.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: An experiment sounds a lot more involved than what I'm doing.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Probably, yes — I'll let you know how many people I manage to rope in.

script.speaker: Dr Fenwick
script.text: Rope in properly, with consent forms, not literally off the street.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Great, I'll start designing it this week.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Are we nearly done? I promised I'd meet someone at four.

script.speaker: Dr Fenwick
script.text: One last thing for both of you — please send me a one-page outline by the end of next week, so I can check the scope is realistic before you start collecting any data.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Will do, thank you.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Same here, thanks for the help narrowing this down.

script.speaker: Dr Fenwick
script.text: Before you both go — write the methods section before you collect a single data point. If you can't explain clearly how you intend to analyse the results, you are not yet ready to gather them.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: That's good to know before we start, rather than after.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Definitely better than finding out in March.

script.speaker: Dr Fenwick
script.text: Quite. I'll see you both again once the outlines are in.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Thanks — this was more useful than I expected, if I'm honest.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Same. I came in convinced my three categories were the strong part of the proposal.

script.speaker: Dr Fenwick
script.text: They might have been, in a much longer dissertation. Off you both go.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS for each answer.

questions.sentence: Ruth's original topic was considered too ___ for a dissertation
questions.explanation: Ruth says her original plan, looking at loyalty cards and spending generally, is "too broad for a dissertation of this length," which is why it needs narrowing.

questions.sentence: Ruth's final topic focuses only on ___
questions.explanation: Comparing students with older shoppers is rejected as too much extra work, and the supervisor confirms the topic is "student spending specifically, not a comparison across ages."

questions.sentence: Research method chosen for Ruth's dissertation: a ___
questions.explanation: Ruth initially leaned towards interviews but decides "a survey makes more sense here," given the numbers needed, and the supervisor agrees.

questions.sentence: Callum's original plan covered electronics, clothing, and ___
questions.explanation: Callum's first idea spanned "electronics, restaurants, clothing," three categories that the supervisor calls "three studies squeezed into one."

questions.sentence: Callum's final topic centres on the effect of a detailed written ___
questions.explanation: Callum says he trusts "a detailed written comment more than a star rating," which becomes the specific focus of his narrowed topic.

questions.sentence: Research method chosen for Callum's dissertation: an ___
questions.explanation: Callum proposes "a small experiment," showing the same restaurant with and without a detailed comment, and the supervisor agrees this isolates the effect better than a survey.

questions.sentence: Both students must send a one-page ___ by the end of next week
questions.explanation: Dr Fenwick's final instruction is "please send me a one-page outline by the end of next week," so she can check the scope before data collection starts.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.question: Why does Dr Fenwick advise against Ruth comparing two age groups?
options: older shoppers are much harder to recruit for a study of this kind
it requires recruiting two separate samples, adding too much work
loyalty schemes do not apply to older shoppers in the same way
questions.explanation: Dr Fenwick points out that "comparing two groups means recruiting two separate samples, which is a lot of extra work for a dissertation on this timeline."

questions.question: Why does Callum choose restaurants over the other product categories?
options: restaurants are a good deal easier to survey
he keeps returning to that category in his reading
Dr Fenwick suggests that category directly
questions.explanation: Callum explains, "I keep coming back to that in my reading anyway," which is his own reason for narrowing to restaurants, not a suggestion from his supervisor.

questions.question: What must both students do before they start collecting data?
options: send Dr Fenwick a one-page outline
choose a second research method as backup
questions.explanation: Dr Fenwick's closing instruction requires an outline "before you start collecting any data," not a pilot study or a backup method.
